name: Prize crossword No 25,005
preamble: Solutions to asterisked clues are capitally linked, directly or indirectly, and are not further defined.

clue.text: Takes the edge off storing ripe fruit for models

indicators.note: a fruit is a product grown out of something, so these letters are worked up into a new form
to store something is to keep it inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: to blunt a blade is to take its edge off
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A cook dulls a knife while keeping ripe fruit to use as artists' models for a still life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fruit' looks like part of the still life, but here it means the product of the letters before it, worked up into a new form.
explanation.definitionFit: Blueprints are detailed plans or templates that something is built from, which is the sense of models as patterns to copy.

indicators.note: something changed has been altered, so these letters are put in a different order
one thing being in another means it sits inside it

blocks.note: the prefix at the front of the word, split off and taken as written
a moment is a point of time

explanation.surface: Something has stayed exactly as it was at a fixed point in time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unchanged' must be read as two parts: its prefix, then 'changed' acting on that prefix. The station takes its name from the Monument to the Great Fire of London.
explanation.definitionFit: As an asterisked clue it has no definition; the preamble links it with the other London Underground stations in the puzzle.

clue.text: * Proceed without having water in the eye

indicators.note: 'without' in its old sense of outside, so one piece wraps round the other

blocks.note: to march is to proceed on foot
blear eyes are dim and watery

explanation.surface: Someone is told to carry on walking without tears in their eyes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' reads as lacking but means outside here. MARBLE ARCH is a London Underground station at the west end of Oxford Street, named after the monumental arch there.
explanation.definitionFit: As an asterisked clue it has no definition; the preamble links it with the other London Underground stations in the puzzle.

blocks.note: A boy's name, short for Stanley
the Sir Thomas who was Henry VIII's chancellor and wrote Utopia

explanation.surface: A page or servant boy is found for a knight called Sir Thomas.
explanation.walkthrough: STANMORE is the northern terminus of the Jubilee line on the London Underground.
explanation.definitionFit: As an asterisked clue it has no definition; the preamble links it with the other London Underground stations in the puzzle.

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it

blocks.note: ghi, or ghee, is clarified butter used in Indian cooking
a range is the limits within which something varies
L-plates, the learner plates on a British car, give two Ls

explanation.surface: Someone sets limits on how much fat goes on the dinner plates.
explanation.walkthrough: L-plates are the red L signs a British learner driver must show front and back. GRANGE HILL is a Central line station in Essex, also the name of a long-running children's TV school drama.
explanation.definitionFit: As an asterisked clue it has no definition; the preamble links it with the other London Underground stations in the puzzle.

indicators.note: going around something means enclosing it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: a chill is a spell of cold
taken as written
a newspaper such as the Guardian speaks of itself as 'we' in its editorials

explanation.surface: A stammering complaint that the Guardian newspaper office is freezing.
explanation.walkthrough: The stutter 'G-Guardian' supplies a lone G before the paper itself, which as the setter's own newspaper is the editorial 'we'. CHIGWELL is a Central line station in Essex.
explanation.definitionFit: As an asterisked clue it has no definition; the preamble links it with the other London Underground stations in the puzzle.

blocks.note: b. is the standard abbreviation for born
lithe means supple and flexible

explanation.surface: Someone is glad to have been born naturally flexible.
explanation.walkthrough: B for born is the abbreviation used in biographies and family trees.
explanation.definitionFit: Blithe is a literary word for cheerful and carefree, a straightforward synonym of happy.

blocks.note: a look is someone's appearance
after means subsequently, later on

explanation.surface: Advice to tend to how you look later on.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a single instruction about grooming, but it splits into a definition and two plain synonyms.
explanation.definitionFit: To look after someone is the everyday phrasal verb for tending, minding or caring for them.

blocks.note: 'the guy will' is 'he will', contracted to he'll
love is nil in tennis scoring, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A man's opening line promises he will fall in love.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in he'll is dropped, as crosswords ignore punctuation. Love as O comes from the zero score in tennis.
explanation.definitionFit: Hello is the ordinary word said on meeting someone, so it is a greeting in itself.

clue.text: Old, old city with prohibition from stockbroker belt

blocks.note: ex- means former or old, as in ex-wife
Ur was the ancient Sumerian city in Mesopotamia
a ban is a prohibition

explanation.surface: An ancient city has a ban on the commuter belt where City financiers live.
explanation.walkthrough: The stockbroker belt is the British name for the wealthy commuter towns outside London, especially in Surrey, where City workers live.
explanation.definitionFit: Exurban describes the prosperous semi-rural zone beyond the suburbs, which is precisely where the stockbroker belt lies.

blocks.note: nigh is an old word for near
a tie is another garment

explanation.surface: One item of clothing hanging next to another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'another' only makes sense as the definition's partner: it means another garment, the TIE.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightie is a nightdress, a loose garment worn in bed, so it is one particular item of clothing.

clue.text: Man of authority in relation to woman and bird

blocks.note: re means concerning, in relation to
Eve, the first woman, a common crossword woman

explanation.surface: An official is in some relationship with a woman and a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: Three readings meet: a medieval official, the charade of RE and EVE, and a female wading bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A reeve was a local magistrate or manor steward in medieval England, and the reeve is also the female of the ruff, a sandpiper.

clue.text: Glees composed in romances with no superior

indicators.note: to compose is to put together afresh, so these letters are set in a new order
one thing being in another means it sits inside it

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
to romance is to tell fanciful untrue stories, that is lies

explanation.surface: Part-songs written into love stories with nobody above them.
explanation.walkthrough: A glee is an unaccompanied part-song, which makes 'composed' look like musical writing. 'romances' is a verb meaning tells tall tales.
explanation.definitionFit: A liege is a feudal lord, so someone liegeless owes allegiance to no overlord and has no superior.

clue.text: Joints with (briefly) fabulous smell go off

indicators.note: said briefly means cut short, so only the start of the word is kept
to go off is to explode or turn bad, so these letters break up and re-form

blocks.note: fab is the clipped slang form of fabulous
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Cuts of meat with a wonderful aroma start to spoil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go off' fits the meat picture as rotting, but it is the signal, and 'go' does double duty as part of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A joint is a large cut of meat for roasting, and legs of lamb are a classic example of such joints.

clue.text: Man with brush grabbing time to copy king's wrapping

indicators.note: to grab something is to hold it tight, so one piece clutches another inside

blocks.note: a chimney sweep works with brushes
T is the abbreviation for time
to ape is to copy or imitate
R stands for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A chimney sweep snatches a moment to imitate the wrapping on a royal present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'king's' reads as the owner of the wrapping, but it only adds R. A sweet paper is the British term for the wrapper round a single sweet, that is a candy.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet paper is the small twist of paper or foil round a sweet, so it is a type of wrapping.

indicators.note: trouble is disorder and disturbance, so these letters are thrown out of order

blocks.note: taken as written, every letter to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An evening on which everyone ends up in bother, perhaps a rowdy night out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' looks like part of the phrase 'get into trouble', but it is fodder too. NOTTING HILL GATE is a London Underground station in west London.
explanation.definitionFit: As an asterisked clue it has no definition; the preamble links it with the other London Underground stations in the puzzle.

clue.text: Pansy's love in it - nothing doing?

blocks.note: first meaning: the wild pansy's old name is love-in-___, so 'it' is the word that completes it
second meaning: the state of having nothing to do

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a pansy's romance amounts to anything at all.
explanation.walkthrough: Love-in-idleness is the folk name for the wild pansy, the flower whose juice Oberon uses in A Midsummer Night's Dream; 'it' stands for the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: Idleness is the condition of not working or being occupied, which is what 'nothing doing' describes.

indicators.note: something between two others is flanked by them on both sides

blocks.note: a.m. marks the morning, and two mornings give it twice
er is the sound of hesitating
sh is the call for silence

explanation.surface: Pauses and quiet fill the gap between one morning and the next.
explanation.walkthrough: AMERSHAM is a town in Buckinghamshire at the far end of the Metropolitan line, the Underground's most distant station.
explanation.definitionFit: As an asterisked clue it has no definition; the preamble links it with the other London Underground stations in the puzzle.

clue.text: Ball carrier on bird's back in the sun needing polisher

indicators.note: going back means going the other way, so these letters run in the opposite direction
one thing on another means placed right after it
one thing being in another means it sits inside it

blocks.note: a golf tee holds the ball
an owl is a bird
Sol is the Latin name for the sun

explanation.surface: A bird sunning itself with a ball on its back needs a polish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bird's back' looks like a body part, but it means the bird written backwards. Sol, the sun, then wraps the TEE and reversed bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Steel wool is a pad of fine steel filaments used for scouring and burnishing surfaces, so it is a polisher.

clue.text: * From the US to Northern Ireland

indicators.note: taken from a phrase means drawn out of its letters, which run on across word breaks

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of 'the' to the start of 'Northern'

explanation.surface: A journey from America on to Northern Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ireland' just completes the picture; EUSTON is the London main-line terminus and Underground station from which trains left for the boats to Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: As an asterisked clue it has no definition; the preamble links it with the other London Underground stations in the puzzle.

blocks.note: a small dark goose
a hybrid of two breeds

explanation.surface: Is this goose a crossbreed?
explanation.walkthrough: The two parts are taken in reverse order of the clue. BRENT CROSS is a Northern line station in north London, beside a big shopping centre.
explanation.definitionFit: As an asterisked clue it has no definition; the preamble links it with the other London Underground stations in the puzzle.

a balm is a soothing healing ointment

explanation.surface: A little laughter in a doctor, the best medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: BALHAM is a Northern line station in south London, made famous by Peter Sellers's spoof travelogue 'Balham, Gateway to the South'.

blocks.note: the Aral Sea in central Asia
the sen is a small Japanese coin

clue.text: Isle is a new region of Europe

indicators.note: something new has been made afresh, so these letters take a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An island turns out to be a newly formed area of the continent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Isle' tempts towards an island answer, but it is only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Silesia is a historical area of central Europe, now mostly in Poland, so it is a region of Europe.

clue.text: Fishy move around Buckingham Palace by my leader

indicators.note: a leader comes at the front, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: Buckingham Palace's postcode district is SW1, with the 1 read as I
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Something suspicious happens near the palace under my boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fishy' suggests suspicious, but the definition is the way a fish moves. London postcodes such as SW1 name areas, so 'around' the palace is its district.
explanation.definitionFit: Swimming is how fish propel themselves through water, so a swim is the movement typical of a fish.
